subject: photosynthesis
title: Photosynthesis: Earth's Solar Factory
summary: Light energy becomes sugar and oxygen—and feeds almost every food web.

keys.prompt: What does photosynthesis convert, and what does it release?
keys.answer: It uses light energy to turn CO2 and water into sugars (food) and releases oxygen as a by-product.

keys.prompt: Where in a plant cell does photosynthesis happen, and what pigment catches light?
keys.answer: In chloroplasts. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue and red light and reflects green, which is why leaves look green.

keys.prompt: Why does ocean plankton matter as much as forests for oxygen production?
keys.answer: NOAA estimates roughly half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from phytoplankton.

cards.title: Your lunch is leftover sunlight
cards.text: A burger, a salad, even a fish taco traces back to organisms that trapped sunlight. Photosynthesis is how that energy entered the food web in the first place.

cards.question: Scientists estimate ocean photosynthesis produces about what share of Earth's oxygen production?
cards.reveal: Roughly half. Tiny phytoplankton punch far above their size—and one bacterium, Prochlorococcus, may alone account for up to about 20% of biosphere oxygen production.

cards.title: The core reaction
cards.text: During photosynthesis, plants and phytoplankton absorb carbon dioxide and use sunlight to combine CO2 with water, forming sugars and releasing oxygen. NASA writes the simplified reaction as CO2 + H2O + energy → CH2O + O2.
cards.example: That sugar becomes the fuel for building leaves, wood, and the food animals eat.

cards.title: Chloroplasts and chlorophyll
cards.text: In plants and algae, the work happens inside chloroplasts. Embedded in their membranes is chlorophyll, the pigment that absorbs light energy. Chlorophyll a absorbs blue and red wavelengths strongly; green is mostly reflected or transmitted, so leaves look green.

why.q: Why absorb blue and red instead of every color equally?
why.a: Pigments only absorb specific wavelengths. Chlorophyll's chemistry is tuned to blue and red; the unused green is what reaches your eyes.

examples_by_interest.golf: Say… the deep green of a fairway is chlorophyll reflecting the wavelengths it does not use for photosynthesis.
examples_by_interest.soccer: Say… a sunlit field looks green because chlorophyll is bouncing green light while capturing blue and red.
examples_by_interest.business: Say… chlorophyll is like a solar panel tuned to certain wavelengths; unused green light is the 'waste light' you see.
examples_by_interest.space: Say… from orbit, green continents are a chlorophyll signal—NASA even tracks plant growth from space.

cards.title: Light first, sugar next
cards.text: Photosynthesis is not one click. First, light-dependent reactions in the chloroplast capture sunlight, split water, and release oxygen while storing energy in short-term carriers. Then plants use that stored energy to build carbohydrate molecules from CO2.
cards.example: NASA summarizes the net result: CO2 + water + energy → sugar + O2. OpenStax details how light absorption by chlorophyll drives the first half.

cards.title: Half the oxygen story is invisible
cards.text: Phytoplankton are microscopic marine algae (and some bacteria) with chlorophyll. They float where sunlight reaches. NOAA estimates roughly half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean—mostly these drifters. Land forests matter hugely too; the split is about half and half for production.
cards.example: Prochlorococcus, the smallest photosynthetic organism known, may produce up to ~20% of the oxygen in our biosphere—more than all tropical rainforests combined, by that estimate.

cards.question: If you were designing a closed space habitat, what would photosynthesis need to keep people alive—and what could still go wrong even if plants grew?
nudges: List inputs (light, CO2, water, nutrients) and outputs (O2, food).
NOAA notes marine life also consumes much of the oxygen the ocean produces—balance matters.

questions.q: What is the best summary of photosynthesis?

options.text: Light energy converts CO2 and water into sugars and releases O2
options.why: Yes—that is the core NASA/biology summary.

options.text: Plants pull oxygen from soil and store it as sugar
options.why: Oxygen released comes from splitting water in the light reactions, not from soil air.

options.text: Heat alone turns water into food
options.why: The energy source is light captured by pigments, not heat alone.

options.text: Roots breathe in sugar from rocks
options.why: Sugars are built in chloroplasts from CO2 and water using light energy.

questions.q: Why do most leaves look green?

options.text: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light and reflects green
options.why: OpenStax: chlorophyll a absorbs ends of the visible spectrum, not green.

options.text: Leaves paint themselves with green dye from soil
options.why: The green is reflected light from chlorophyll, not soil dye.

options.text: Green light is the only color plants can use
options.why: They mostly use blue and red; green is the color they use least.
Leaf color comes from pigments inside the leaf.

questions.q: About what share of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean?

options.why: NOAA's estimate for ocean production is about 50%.
Land plants produce a large share as well.
Oceans both produce and consume; production from plankton is huge.

sources.title: The Carbon Cycle
sources.supports: Plants absorb CO2 and sunlight to make glucose/sugars; plants and phytoplankton combine CO2 + water + energy → sugar + O2; foundation of the fast carbon cycle; animals eat plants/plankton for that energy.

sources.title: How much oxygen comes from the ocean?; What are phytoplankton?
sources.supports: ~Half of oxygen production from ocean; phytoplankton with chlorophyll; Prochlorococcus up to ~20%; marine life consumes roughly as much as ocean produces; atmospheric O2 accumulated over hundreds of millions of years.
